For the Department of Public Works, I hare a statement from the chief eugineer. He says :
There are two ways of measuring the quantity of material dredged, one being measurement in situ and the other, scow measurement.
It has always been the custom of the department to adopt the latter, as it is considered that with faithful inspectors in charge of the different works, the quantities returned are as near as practicable absolutely correct and therefore fair and just both to the department and to the contractor. Moreover, the in situ mode of measurement necessitates extensive and most accurate surveys before the beginning of the work, monthly during its execution and after its final completion, which accurate surveys of course, would entail such a large expenditure in the way of additional staff, as to be, in my opinion, prohibitive, In fact, the expenditure for surveying would, in some eases, be as great as the cost of the dredging itself.
Moreover, I am of opinion, that it is practically impossible to return accurately, by this way of measurement, the actual quantity of dredging performed, as the surface dredged would have to be entirely covered with soundings, say every five feet apart, in order to arrive, even then, at only an approximation.
For these reasons, I am of opinion that the method adopted by the department is certainly the best, providing of course, that the inspectors be competent and thoroughly reliable.
Respectfully submitted, EUGENE D. LAFLEUR, Chief Engineer.
I should add that the dredging work in the two departments is entirely different. In the Railway Department it usually extends over but a narrow area, being mostly confined to canal work, while in the Public Works Department the area is very much larger, in connection with the dredging of harbours and rivers and the like.

On Sunday night or Monday morning of last week an accident occurred by the derailing and immersion in a lake of a mail car near Kenora, and on the Wednesday following I asked the Postmaster General if he had any information about it and he replied that he had not. Since then the Postmaster General has been good enough to inform me that the information had reached the department on the 1st of June, that "a portion of the mails had been rescued and had been spread out and dried and forwarded to their destination with a note stating what happened to them. The fact remains that a portion of those mails may nof yet have been delivered, and I was expecting letters myself about that date. I have since received two letters. One of them was inclosed in a wrapper from the Ottawa post office stating that it had been received in a damaged condition, at Ottawa, Ontario. That is all the information I got to account for the damaged condition in which this letter, which was posted on the 23rd of May at the town of Moosomin, reached me. The other letter had a note across it stating that it was damaged by water owing to a railway accident near Kenora, Ontario. Of course, I realize that that is practically all that the Post Office Department could do at the moment ; but it would be much more satisfactory to me if I had known at the time the accident happened that the mails coming from the Northwest had been delayed in consequence of an accident. It would have been still more satisfactory if I were aware that the persons in the Northwest who had addressed letters to me knew that an accident had happened to the mail car on which their letters,had been conveyed. Last year I saw a very brief item in a paper stating that a mail car had been destroyed by fire in the Northwest several days before, and I had no idea whether some important letter of mine might not have been in that mail car and
had not reached its destination. It seems to me that when accidents of this kind happen, the proper course would be for notices to be sent to all the post offices from which bags had been sent by the destroyed mail car, so that people sending important communications would have the earliest possible notice if their communications had been destroyed or damaged or delayed in transit. It must be evident to everybody that accidents of this kind may be fraught with very serious consequences to private individuals using the mails. A good many years ago I suffered a great deal of inconvenience from the fact that a letter disappeared, and I could only guess that it must have been destroyed with a mail car that had been burned, as some time later I heard had been the case. When such a thing happens I think the Postmaster General should give notice to the post office from which letters conveyed on the mail car were despatched, stating that it had been burned.

person as his deputy to perform his duties as judge during the time in which he was engaged in the work of this commission. No action however was taken by the government, although a Bill had been placed on the Order Paper early in March and upon that Bill being presented to this House on the 14th May it was passed immediately with very little discussion and with some slight amendments and has gone from this House to the Senate. I do not know what its fortune has been in the Senate, nor do I know whether it is in a position to receive the assent of the Governor General. At all events it left this House on the same day that its second reading was brought on ; that is to say, on the 14th day of May last. Now, the allegations of the commissioners with respect to the Department of Marine and Fisheries were of a sufficiently serious character to evoke from the government, on the 26th day of March last, the statement that an immediate and effective inquiry would be made. Nearly three months have elapsed and nothing has been done except the examination of two of the commissioners before Mr. Justice Cassels, and possibly the examination of one or two other persons. It seems to me that this is a matter of some urgency. The opposition in parliament would be justified, without taking a very extreme position at all, in insisting that the work of that commission should be prosecuted to a conclusion and its report presented to parliament before the conclusion of this session and before any further supplies should be granted to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I think that would be a perfectly proper and constitutional position for the opposition to take. We have not announced any such determination up to the present time, but I think it is only fair and right for me to say to the Prime Minister that this is a matter of urgency, that the government themselves have recognized it as a matter of great urgency and that the very slight progress which has been made in the prosecution of the inquiry does not reflect credit upon the administration of the government, nor does it indicate any great desire on the part of the government to facilitate these proceedings. That is all I have to say as to that particular subject. It might be elaborated at much greater length, but I think the Prime Minister will understand thoroughly, from the few words I have spoken, my view with regard to the matter.
'There is one other subject in connection with the report of the commission to which I also desire to call attention. Two of the commissioners were	examined-Messrs.
Fyshe and Bazin-and I believe that very little was elicited from them beyond the statement that they stood by the report and that they did not consider themselves subject to cross-examination with respect

to the grounds upon which they had made that report. They took, In effect, the position that all the information which they had obtained was available to the commissioner himself, that it could be procured by him and that it was not very consonant with the position which they had occupied as members of a royal commission that they should be cross-examined before another commissioner as to the grounds upon which they had reached their conclusions. But there was one officer, not a member of that commission, but an officer of parliament, who might very well have been called and called at the earliest possible stage before Mr. Justice Cassels, and I am at a loss to know why it was that the counsel acting for the government in this inquiry failed to have their attention directed to the necessity of calling Mr. Fraser, the Auditor General. As an example of the service that he might have been able to give in the prosecution of the inquiry, let me call the attention of the government to the evidence which Mr. FrSfeer has already given before the royal commission upon the subject of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The evidence which I shall quote is at page 1309 of the evidence reported to parliament and printed :

I do not wish to add anything to what Mr. Fraser has said in his evidence, except that it is exactly the point that we had raised in respect of the investigation concerning the ' Arctic ' expedition. In that case there were certificates as to quantities and as to prices. It was urged by the Conservative members of that committee that we should go behind and investigate the cor-

rectness of these certificates and that the committee should hear evidence of persons who had made an examination of the stock remaining in the vessel after the expedition. The certificates were, so far as I recollect, considered to be prima facie evidence at least of the amount on board and there was not much investigation of the actual accuracy of the certificate. It is true that some persons were called who testified that certificates were given and they were all right so far as they knew, but I am making the same point that the Auditor General makes in his evidence that there as well as in the every day business of the government, the certificate is not good unless the officer certifying actually knows that the goods were supplied, that the prices are fair and that the expenditure is therefore a reasonable one.
There is another matter which concerns, but not so closely, the report of this royal commission. I shall not again refer to the parts of the report in which the commissioners point out that some better system should be devised with respect to the statistics of the country. It is pointed out in this report that the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Customs both prepare blue-books containing reports of the trade and commerce of the country, and other important statistics. It is suggested ' by the commission that this work should be done in a more thorough and uniform way and they make several suggestions. Among other things they suggest that the publication might be supervised by the joint committee of parliament entrusted with the printing of parliamentary documents.
Certain correspondence has been forwarded to me by the government of British Columbia. I shall not quote it in full but shall merely state its purport. On April 2, 1908, the assistant secretary of the Bureau of Provincial Information of British Columbia asked the Department of Customs for a statement of the total exports and imports of British Columbia for the last fiscal year. The details were asked for if it was possible to give them, but the totals were asked for in the meantime. No answer having being received, on April 27, more than three weeks afterwards, a telegram was sent to the Department of Customs to which, on the same day, a reply was received from the Department of Customs stating that the letter of April 2 could not be found and asking that a duplicate should be sent. A reply to that telegram was forwarded on the same day from the office of the secretary of the Bureau of Provincial Information of British Columbia repeating the request for the total of the imports and exports of British Columbia for the last fiscal year. On April 28, the Department of Customs telegraphed to the provincial secretary of British Columbia that the. report 309
had been mailed on the 21st of April and the letter of the 21st of April, which arrived shortly afterwards, contained the information as to the exports and imports of that province during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1908. That letter was acknowledged on April 28, and a further request was made for the details of these statements, it being alleged by the secretary of the Bureau of Provincial Information of British Columbia that people were constantly asking for the quantities and values of imports and exports of different classes of goods. On May 7, that letter was acknowledged by the Department of Customs and it wras stated that some time must elapse before the figures would be available, but that a note had been made of the matter and the department would endeavour to comply with the request at the earliest possible date. On May 14, a letter was written by the Commissioner of Customs to the assistant secretary of the Bureau of Information. The letter is as follows :
Ottawa, May 14, 1908. Frank I. Clarke, Esq.,
Assistant Secretary 'Bureau of Provincial 'Information, Victoria, British Columbia.

Upon looking further into the matter and consulting the chief clerk in charge of statistics, I am advised that the preparation of such a statement would entail a great amount of labour and consume considerable time in its preparation, necessitating the withdrawal of clerks from their regular duties while so engaged, and as the staff is fully engaged in the preparation of the annual report and other parliamentary papery it is impossible to prepare such a statement unless by assigning the work to special officers to be done after regular office hours, for which they would expect to be compensated.
In the circumstances. I am writing to state that if yon are willing to compensate these men while so engaged in overtime work, the statement will be got readv as^ soon as possible. I estimate the cost will he about seventy-five dollars.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,

I am not disposed to minimize the difficulties in the preparation of these statistics directly after the close of the fiscal year, but it does seem a matter of regret if information of that kind cannot be furnished to the government of a province who asked for this reasonable public information, without imposing upon them a certain charge for furnishing it. I dare say the same system has been carried out in the past, indeed I am disposed to believe the Minister of Customs has made some improvements in the preparation of statistics, but it is an unfortunate condition of affairs that figures of that kind should not be available at the very earliest possible moment ; and without desiring in any way to unduly criticise the record of the government in this respect I would submit to the Prime Minister that the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce should undertake a reorganization of this statistical branch at the very earliest possible moment so that not only for the provincial governments but for all the citizens of the country who may desire reasonable information of that kind such reasonable information would be forthcoming without the necessity of imposing a tax or charge upon either the provincial government or any person or corporation who may desire information of that character with regard to an important public subject.

With regard to the latter part of the information sought by my hon. friend, I have only to say that it is a purely departmental matter as to which I am sure the Minister of Customs, as soon as he is in his seat, will be able to give some answer to my hon. friend. I am sorry to say that personally I could not say anything at present upon this point.
With regard to the other matter, that is to say the inquiry of my hon. friend as to the investigation of the Civil Service, my hon. friend is aware that Mr. Justice Cas-sels has adjourned his inquest, I think to a certain date in the present month.

lion. G. E. FOSTER (North Toronto). There seems to me to be an expensive and unnecessary reduplication of publications with reference to the trade and other statistics. There is also a lack of agreement between the publications as they are issued by the different departments. The Trade and Navigation reports are issued by the Minister of Customs and the Trade and Commerce reports by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Any person taking these up and arranging a series of comparative statements or reports from one of them finds when ho refers to the other that for the very same year and the very same period there is a disagreement in the total figures, and in order to be accurate and save himself he has to state from which of these returns he takes the figures so that he may not be confronted with a statement for the same year which he cannot substantiate from the report he has used. Besides that there is a complete reduplication of matter in the Trade and Navigation report and the Trade and Commerce report in certain particulars. Both of these are very bulky and costly volumes, and I do not see why it is necessary to have a reduplication of the very same information in these two large volumes issued by different departments of the same government and simply issued by different departments. The Trade and Commerce Department issues a series of monthly reports. They call them bulletins. They are large reports, they are costly, but the trouble about them is that when you receive them they are two, three or four months late. To whom are they distributed? They may come to the members of parliament but they are practically of no use to them, the member of parliament may occasionally use some figures from them if he is preparing speeches, but a member of parliament depends upon the yearly reports. It is with yearly statements that he is particularly engaged. Then where do these go? It is supposed they are distributed to boards of trade and merchants, &c., but there again

the trouble is they are two or three or four months behind the time, and the information they give is, 1 think, of very little practical benefit, at least I have talked with people who get them who say that. Now, these cost a lot of money. Again you have the abstract which is now issued. Your census report is made up and is distributed in complete form and also in bulletin form. These figures come to the members of parliament, to the men who make a study of statistics and to all those who propose to use them. Then again there is the statistical abstract, the Year-book of Canada as it is called. The statistical abstract for the last two years'has been very largely an extension of the figures that have been published in the census report. It is, I was going to say, absolutely useless for the purpose for which a Year-book is compiled. Any man who wishes to study these figures gets them in the reports of the Census Department and then he takes up the Year-book thinking he is going to get fresh information but finds that a large portion of it is available in other forms. A very large proportion is taken up with a reduplication of the census returns. Another very large part is taken up with bolus bolus transfers from the Trade and Navigation Report or from the Trade and Commerce Report and the figures of Trade and Commerce in their different forms. You get absolutely nothing that you do not get in the Trade and Commerce Report, and you get it not in its full form but in a necessarily imperfect form. Then you get certain statistics with reference to some of the other departments which are culled from their reports. A condensation of some of these may be useful but my contention is that in the first place there is a large amount of statistical work done by different departments, each doing it separately, and that there is a useless and expensive duplication. It seems to me to be perfectly useless to publish a Y'ear-book which is merely a duplication of parliamentary reports which have already appeared. Your Year-book does not give anything fresh because it is a year or a year and a half behind the times. The Year-book ought to be fresh and up to date, which I am sorry to say the present Yearbook is not. The kind of statistics we want we don't get, and the kind we do not want we get measured up in two or three different forms. It would be a good thing for the government to appoint a commission of three or four competent people who are in the departments and let them look up the whole question of statistical reports so as to provide that there shall be no duplication, and if possible that they shall be brought up to date. When we compare our statistics with those issued in the United States the disparity in usefulness and efficiency is very apparent.

Sometimes I send these monthly reports of the Department of Customs back to the distribution office as I find them of no practical value. The last report for March, the end of the fiscal year, was placed in my desk yesterday and as that report gives a return for the full twelve months of the year I found it quite useful and a moment ago I forwarded it to a manufacturer in my county who I knew would be interested in it. But I would not trouble him by sending him the reports of the previous months because they would not give him an opportunity of ascertaining how the trade of the country was. I have often been confused myself with the superabundance of statistics we have. The report of the Trade and Commerce Department and the Trade and Navigation returns vary very greatly and are very confusing. I understand that the report of the Trade and Commerce Department gives the entire imports regardless of whether they are for home consumption or not, while the Trade and Navigation returns classify the imports. I do not think the members of this House would be one whit worse off if the entire reports of the Trade and Commerce Department were ignored for it is only a useless expense to print and duplicate the information they contain. I rarely find any good use for the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce although I am very fond of studying the Trade and Navigation returns in which I generally get all the information I want.
I regret that the Minister of Customs is not in his place to-day-I am not finding any fault with that because I was absent myself last week, and I presume he is absent to-day for the same reason-but had he been here I would point out to him that the monthly reports of his department would be very much more useful if they included another column giving the amount of duties paid under the general tariff, the preferential tariff, and the surtax. I do not think it would add to the trouble or expense if that information were supplied, and I would ask the minister were he here to directions officers to set out in these reports what duties had been collected. More especially would I like to see that information in the last monthly report for the fiscal year, for then it would answer all the purposes of the complete volume of the Trade and Navigation returns which will not be published for perhaps six months after the end of the fiscal year. This w'ould enable the members of the House during recess to study these matters so as to be able to intelligently discuss them when parliament meets again. With regard to the Yearbook.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It's no good.

It may be useful to some, but when I get it, it is too old to be

of any use to me, and lienee I probably do not refer to it once a year. Frequently it may be used to compare one year with another, but generally speaking I have found it very useless.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce might repudiate it as he did two or three years ago.

Of course, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has practically nothing or very little to do, and if we were to deprive him of the publication of that volume, his department might be rendered almost useless, and there would then be no justification for paying him a salary of $7,000 a year and keeping a highly paid deputy minister.

The question of the duplication of statistical reports is one which I have referred to on a previous occasion, and like the hon. member for Halton, I am sorry that the Minister of Customs is not here to-day. If the reports of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the' Trade and Navigation returns were intelligently consolidated, they would be very much more useful to the members of the House and to the public than they are at present.
I cannot understand why it is necessary to go to the expense of issuing two reports so nearly alike. Besides these reports, there is the Statistical Year-book. This book, in its present form, is less useful than it formerly was. There has been omitted from it seventy-two important subjects which appeared in the former Year-book, and in order to get this information one has to go over the reports of various departments of the government and to search the books, periodicals and governmental reports published in foreign countries. I suppose that the object in reducing the size of the Year-book of Canada was to have members and the public refer to the reports of the various departments of the government; but as a matter of fact that is not practicable. People will not look through such voluminous reports. Most people want information in more convenient form. It seems to me that we have gone a little further than is necessary in the way of governmental publications. The whole question should be reviewed, by a commission or otherwise, and the reports made of more practical service than they are at present. In the Statistical Abstract of the United States there are very many subjects which are not to be found in the Year-book of Canada, but which were previously contained in it. I had a return brought down showing the various matters which are omitted from the present Year-book. Some of these are very important, such as imports and exports and duties per head of the population, imports and exports of foreign goods via Canada, imports and exports of foreign goods via the United States, im-

ports and exports of foreign countries, drawbacks allowed, aggregate trade of the Dominion, average value of imports in three year periods, public debts of foreign countries, provincial debts, &c. I think it would be well for the government to consider whether these subjects should not again be included in the Year-book, and whether the statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Trade and Navigation Returns cannot be consolidated.

I have been in the habit for many years of sending copies of the Dominion Year-book to Public school .teachers and to men in commercial life, who found that it contained valuable information. But since the change has taken place I have been reminded by several that the book has become practically worthless. This book was originally compiled by Mr. George Johnston, who was the best statistician we ever had here j but objection was taken that the book was too large, that it dealt with too many subjects, and some gentlemen were of opinion that Mr. Johnston should be supplanted, and that the book should be compiled by some one else on narrower lines. The government heeded these representations and made a change, and with what result ? That the book has become almost useless. I agree entirely *with what the hon. member for East Toronto has said. The book was formerly a valuable compilation of statistics, and it might be so again if it were properly compiled.

It was my intention to have taken up a matter relating to the Customs Department, but the Minister of Customs is not in his place. I sent him notice yesterday of my intention to take that matter up. Apparently, from what his colleagues say, he has left the city. I find that in my absence the other evening, he took the opportunity of criticising me for being absent. Well, I know of no argument he could apply to myself which would not apply with equal force to the minister. If he has gone to my constituency, as reported, I do not think he was justified in his criticism of me with regard to that same matter. I came down early in the week purposely to take up matters in connection with customs.
I had made a personal request to the minister that he would reserve one item in his estimates on which we might have a general discussion of the affairs of his department. This he did not do and I judge from what I see in ' Hansard ' that it is not the intention of the minister to give me the opportunity I asked for when going away. I shall take the earliest opportunity when he is here to criticise certain acts done in the department and certain parts of its administration. I shall therefore defer the remarks I was going to make until such time as the

minister is here attending to his duties. I thought it was well to explain the situation to the House because I sent him a letter yesterday saying that I was going to make some remarks. *

speechtext: There are three parties at work, one actually running the line and the second taking the topography of the country adjoining the line and the third cutting a way through the woods along the line.
How many men are employed altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our party works in conjunction with the party of the United States. I am informed there are probably about sixty men in the party.
Is that line beihg surveyed right through to the Arctic ocean?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the ultimate intention.
Is there necessity for this work going on up in the Arctic circle?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course the question of boundaries may at any time become important and it is generally considered better to have such questions settled at a time when they are not attracting attention rather than to await the time when they may be attracting attention. A dispute is much more easily settled if it is not allowed to arise. That is the principle we are going on in the case of the ,141st. meridian. As my hon.' friend is probably aware there is a part of that meridian which must be very accurately defined because of the gold mining operations which are going on on both sides of the line. That is a highly mineralized country and we have hopes that gold discoveries may be made in other places, we do not know where, but we think we should he preparing at a reasonable rate of speed and with a reasonable expenditure so that should it at any time be necessary to absolutely know where the boundary is we will know it. It is one of the responsibilities attaching to the ownership of vast territories. and having assumed the responsi-1 bility it must be discharged.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: ilr. KEMP. As I understand, part of the territory is allotted to the United States survey parties and part to the Canadian, they do not work jointly but in alternate positions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They work jointly so that their work is checked. Each checks the work of the other as it proceeds.

I understood they had separate camps and came together at certain points, that we accepted their line for nine or ten miles and they accepted ours for nine or ten miles, that they did not work together.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The system of which my hon. friend speaks is that which prevails on the Alaska coast boundary, an irregular boundary line which divides the strip of Alaska along the Pacific coast from the interior of British Columbia and the Yukon. In that case each country accepts the work done by the party of the other country ; they work in alternate sections, but in that case it is a question of delimitation according to physical features. In the case of the 141st meridian it is a case of accuracy of scientific establishment and in such a case it is considered that the only correct way is that the work of each party should be checked by the other as it is being done.
Is the minister sure the parties can survey as much as 130 miles in a season?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My information is that the work done last season was about 130 miles south from the point where the 141st meridian crosses the Yukon river.

The reason I asked was that in going to the experimental farm the other day I met a man who had been working on that Yukon survey who told me that they were able to do about nine miles a year. I do not know his name but he was one of the men going out there.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend has derived his information from an unreliable source.
Does this item for surveys cover the delimiting of the boundary under the treaty recently signed with reference to which we have not yet received the correspondence ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We will have to ask for a supplementary vote for the work of delimiting the boundary under the new treaty. This vote will cover part of that work but it is not sufficient to cover the expenditure caused by the treaty recently signed.

It seems to me that the House is treated with scant courtesy in being asked for votes to delimit a boundary under treaties when we have not the treaties or the correspondence referring to them in our possession. Surely parlia-
9741	JUNE 3, 1908	9742
ment ought to know under what conditions they are going to delimit tliis boundary. Parliament ought to be informed as to wbat has taken place between the imperial government and the government of the United States in regard to these treaties before it is asked to vote money for delimiting the boundaries. It is going it blind to a great extent and I think somebody ought to make a statement to explain to the House what has been done so that we could know the exact provisions of these treaties. We are voting money and allowing men to go and delimit the boundary without knowing upon what authority beyond the statement that there has been a treaty passed which is binding on Canada but which has not yet been laid upon the table of the House.
The boundary line between Canada and the United States was fixed at the 141st meridian six years ago.

We are talking about the whole boundary between Canada and the United States. As I understand they are going on to delimit the boundary westward from the St. Lawrence river under a treaty that we have not even read in this House and as to which we have no information. I think it is a very unbusinesslike way for parliament to do especially with respect to a matter that concerns the country so much.	[DOT]

I think the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has possibly not been paying as close attention to his duties as he might have. Otherwise, he would have found that the treaty has been laid before parliament. I got it in my desk. I sent several copies out to people in British Columbia who were anxious to see it.
When ?
The day before yesterday.

All I can say is that the minister said that it would have to be printed. He laid it on the table of the House, but it was not printed or distributed and in so far as I know it is not printed or distributed yet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have not received a copy of it yet.
I got mine from the distribution office in the regular way.
You got some advance copies.
No.	'
You must be the white headed boy.

May be I am. Perhaps I am like the man who was born blind and who was cured; he could not say how it happened but he was cured just the
same. I have been informed and I have also read in the coast papers that the Canadian and American Alaska boundary survey parties are held up on the coast due to the fact that there is no money voted to cover the cost of the delimitation of this boundary line. I would like to know if that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend's information is only partially correct. The Canadian par-ties in question have not yet left Ottawa. We have not felt justified in sending them out without an assurance of the funds necessary to pay them. Of course the United States survey party cannot proceed under the agreement that has been made without our survey party being on the ground.

I see that they have had one meeting in Buffalo and that they intend to have another at Toronto. We are providing for the delimitation of the boundary without seeing the treaty under which this is to be done. Parliament ought to be informed of its details before being asked to vote money.

I would like to know what the facts are, Statements are made in the coast papers and it is common talk there apparently that the United States survey parties are at Juneau awaiting the arrival of the Canadian parties both of which were to have met some time in the early part of May to begin the work, but they cannot proceed because of the nonarrival of the Canadian party. When the Alaskan boundary award was made five or six years ago, was it not accepted by both governments that the 141st meridian would be the boundary line between the two countries ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is absolutely correct. The parties should be on the ground, but the United States party, of course, cannot proceed with the work without our party being there. We cannot send them until we get the sanction of parliament. The delimitation of the boundary on the 141st meridian which is the subject of their work is not the subject of the treaty recently signed. The treaty of 1900 provides for a survey of the 141st meridian as the boundary between Alaska and Canada. The exact point at which the meridian crosses the Yukon was determined by astronomical observation in 1906; therefore, the vote which we are asking for now in that particular part has nothing to do with the treaty that is under consideration. The whole of this vote which is now before the House in these main estimates is apportioned amongst the boundary surveys which have been already arranged foi.
Between what points?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The 141st meridian between the Yukon and Alaska; the boundary

between the coast strip of Alaska and Canadian territory : the 49th parallel between the Northern States and the Canadian west, and the boundary between New Brunswick and the State of Maine, coming westerly. The work in these four sections of the boundary is now being done under an agreement and under treaties entered into.
Taking the New Bruns-woslc portion, how many miles are to be delimited there and how many miles have been delimited ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There have been delimited about 65 miles between New York and Quebec and 100 miles between Vermont and Quebec. That part of the line is completed. We are proposing to begin now at the other end of the line between the State of Maine and New Brunswick and it is for that work, commencing at the other end and coming easterly, that we are asking for the money.
Mr. FOSTER, How many miles will that be ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Between 350 and 400 miles remain to be done.
Of the New Brunswick portion ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Between New Brunswick and Maine and the remainder between Quebec and Maine and Quebec and New Hampshire.
Mr. FOSTER, How many miles altogether have to be delimited ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About 550 miles.
Of which how much will be done ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
165 miles.
Mr. FOSTER, And of the New Brunswick portion none has been done ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, they are commencing that now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems a pity that the treaties between Great Britain and the United States were not laid on the table of the House and printed earlier. As I understand it this vote is for the delimitation of the boundary provided for by the Alaskan treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only concern this vote would have with the recent treaty is that if there were a surplus from this vote it would of course go to the delimitation under the new treaty. It could be used for that but we are not asking the vote for that purpose. We will have to ask a supplementary estimate for the purpose of carrying out the terms of the treaty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have not had a copy of this treaty and I should think the distribution of public documents should be '

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
a little more uniform than It appears to
have been in this case.
I sent and got it in the distribution office.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know why it should remain in the distribution office when there have been so many inquiries in the House for it.
Is the survey going on at present ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The parties for the coast boundary have left but the parties for the 141st meridian have not because we did not feel justified in sending them to extreme points where expenses would be great unless we had the sanction of parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And this is the first time this vote has been asked for.

The United States survey parties are cooling their heels in Juneau, Alaska, and our survey parties are doing the same thing around Vancouver and other coast cities. The United States have their men financed and we have no money for our men and so this parliament has "placed itself in a ridiculous position.
This parliament which is in that position has never been asked for a dollar of this money until half past 12 o'clock on this the 3rd day of June, 1908.
I appreciate that.
If the hon. gentleman has any fault to find let him pitch into his minister.

I make no captious criticism, but if parliament has not before been asked for this money it is because day after day this parliament tried to get into Supply and Supply has been blocked. The hon. gentleman from North Toronto knows it, everybody knows it. It is particularly annoying in an international matter of this kind that such should be the case. For weeks our newspapers in British Columbia have been discussing it and the people on the coast understand the reason for it.
This is an important matter ?
It is an important matter.
More important than anything else ?

I do not say it is more important than anything else, but it is more important in the delimitation of the boundary between Canada and the United States in Alaska it should be gone on with because there are gold discoveries taking place all the time, and if Canadian governments for the last 50 years had been

alive to their duty Canada would to-day own Skagway and Lynn canal.
If your Prime Minister had not made the assertion lie did in parliament we might have had a great deal more.

I am endeavouring to treat of this question above party politics and I say we should have the international boundary line delimited because there is a rich country to the north and gold is being found and will be found for years to come and we want to have our flag floating over onr own land so that marauders cannot come as they have in the past and take a considerable portion of onr country, backed up by men like Lord Alvestone. I think it is time the House got this vote through.
So do I.
It should be put through at once.
I agree with you.

It is time also
that our good friends opposite should realize the condition they have placed the country in by blocking the supplies.
You placed it in that position.

Day after day
Supply has been blocked and this is only one instance of the result.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: My hon. friend has taken that line of argument
Meet it fairly.

It can be met fairly in this way. This House has been in session close on seven months, and its work could have been got through a njonth ago. There is no necessity for my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, for whom I have every regard, attempting to draw a red herring across the trail. There is no deliberative assembly, made up of business men, not even a county council, that would not have got through the business a month ago if it laid aside party politics.
Where is your Civil Service Bill, where is your Hudson Bay Railway Bill, where is your Land Bill, where is your Manitoba Boundary Bill?
If every member of the House of Commons took up the amount of time taken up by the hon. member for North Toronto, who seems to be obsessed for talking

I object, Mr. Chairman, to any such language as that being applied to a member of this House. I do not exactly know what the meaning of that word is: but from the fire in the eye of my hon. friend and the way it tripped off his tongue, it is a bad word, and I ask that it be withdrawn.
My good friend is like the fishwife whom Daniel O'Connell called a parallelogram.
Mr. Chairman, I am not like the fishwife, and if the hon. gentleman wants to have a committee of investigation he can have it.

There are some things I would rather not have a committee of investigation on, because some horrible details mjght be spread on the records of this country. If all the members of the House of Commons took up as much time as the hon. member for North Toronto, we would require to be here twelve months. If our hon. friends would simply come to the conclusion to put party politics aside-and X am not saying that, all the fault is on one side-we could finish up the business in a very short time. Here is a case in which tlie United States government have their men in the field waiting for our people to come alongside and do the work. This House met in November last and got into Committee of Supply a week after, and the Supplies have been blocked by our hon. friends opposite from that day to this, and they know it.

I asked my hon. friend to * meet fairly the circumstances detailed by

tlie leader of the opposition. Does he think he has vlone it ?
Of course I have.

Suppose there has been a large amount of talk ; suppose the member who is at present speaking has done a great deal of it; he did no more and no less up to the 15th of May, and on the 45th of May the government, which was supposed to know what was most pressing, got the House into Supply, and instead of' taking up this international business of great importance, took up a number of dispersed public works in cities represented by Grit members in Manitoba and the Northwest, and we passed, with all the obstruction, as it is alleged, votes amounting to $538,000. Does my hon. friend think that if the Minister of the Interior had foreseen the circumstances and put his vote before the House, he could not have carried it when we voted more than double the amount for these public works ? On the 20tli of May we voted $1,104,895, about five times as much as the Minister of the Interior is asking for to-day. Is it reasonable to say that if the minister had taken this international question up on that date he could not have got his $330,00(3 ns well as the other departments got their $1,104,000 ? On the 22nd of May we voted $5,479,110 for the Post Office and on the 1st of June we voted $1,815,000 for the Customs ; and yet we were not asked for this vote. There is nothing but wind in what my hon. friend said. He declares that it is because the opposition obstruct-because a righteous, far-seeing government are not allowed to work their will in any particular -that they are cooling their heels in particular places, and Rritish Columbia knows the reason why. British Columbia is inhabited by intelligent people, and I am not bound to maintain that the most intelligent of its population have found their way into this House ; and the people of British Columbia, when that state of facts is placed before them, will ask the question : If these gentleman had any foresight as to what was more important, why did they not bring this vote on one of these dates? Besides, the Minister of the Interior has had one-eighth of that amount for nearly two months.
After this excellent lecture from the hon. gentleman I will trust that he will apply a little of his own sophistry to his own case.
Why does my hon. friend use the word ' sophistry V Is it a fact or is it not what I have quoted? Does he deny the statement? If he does not, it is not sophistry, but plain, hard facts.

I have not been in the House so long as my hon. friend, and he has more liberty to interrupt than I have and he has more skill in suiting the rules Mr. FOSTER
of debate to his own purposes. But I want to tell him in reply to his satire, that nobody in the province of British Columbia has made use of his intelligence on the floor of this House to abuse his opportunities as my hon. friend has. I do not think that anybody from that province has ever attempted, for my part I have never attempted. to belittle any member of this House. I always try to play the game fair. I am a new member compared with the hon. gentleman. He is an old timer, he has sat around the council board of His Majesty and is a Privy Councillor, and I think he should be above making a statement like that.
Like what?
A statement reflecting upon the intelligence of any member from the province of British Columbia.
I did uot do that. I could not do it.

I want to tell my hon. friend that although in his opinion those coming from the province of British Columbia may not be very intelligent, we know how to hold our own, and we have never had to leave that province to find a seat in another one.
Your experience has not been so long.

No, and my planks are not very thin and I have not had to run so far as the hon. gentleman. I have not been obliged to run about looking for a seat, and consequently have not had the same experience, but I tell my hon. friend that he should be above that kind of thing. Let me tell him, in all fairness, that we should come down to business and forget party politics for a while and get through with it.

I came in a few moments ago and have been since wondering what the item before the committee is. Judging by the speech of the hon. gentleman, the subject before us must be a very varied one because he has adverted to many things. What surprises me is that when he complains of our not getting the work, he should waste so much valuable time in talking of something not at all pertinent to the question. He has no right to make any complaint when he himself is using up the valuable time of the House by obstructing its business. I hardly think he can find fault with my applying that word to his own conduct, because, so far as I could understand, he did not appear to be addressing himself to any particular question before the committee at all, and I was surprised that you, Mr. Chairman, did not call him to order and refuse to allow him to air his eloquence in telling us about Hie fine people who come from British Columbia. We know that there are lots of

fine people in that province and that the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpher-son) is one of the finest. No doubt he represents his constituency very well, but this is not the time for him to raise his voice on behalf of Vancouver. That surely cannot be an item in the estimates, and I trust that when he again rises in his place to delay the committee and call its attention away from the practical question before us you will draw his attention to that fact. Self laudation is not what we are here for. I am anxious that we should go on and I hope we shall do some business this afternoon. We are anxious to give the Department of the Interior and some of the other departments some money. Some of the ministers are complaining that they have not got money, but they have not asked for it. Here is the Minister of Militia complaining when he has not asked for a dollar. It is time for ministers to find fault with the opposition when they bring down their estimates. We cannot vote their estimates through until they are placed before the committee. I fail to see the point of the hon. gentleman's criticism, and I trust, Mr. Chairman, that you will watch him this afternoon in case he should rise again and take such another stand as he has done. In such an event I hope that you will keep him down to the point and force him to confine his discussion to the question before the committee. I may be called to order because I have not been discussing the question, but, as a matter of fact, I do not know what the question is and consequently I am not able to discuss it. May I ask what is the item before us?
It is the salaries of the technical officers of the Dominion Astronomical Observatory.

Now that the hon. member for British Columbia (Mr. Maepher-son) has ceased his obstruction, I hope to get some information. I have now traced the boundary lines-New Brunswick and the United States, Quebec and New York, Quebec and Vermont. What other boundary line is it that we are delimiting?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The forty-ninth parallel. At present the party is working on the international boundary between Montana and Alberta, eastward from the summit of the Rockies. The work was completed in previous years from the summit of the Rockies westward to the Pacific coast.
About how many miles?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About 410 miles.
And the two sections now being worked are Montana and Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the line between Montana and Alberta now being run will be continued eastward between Saskatchewan and Montana, Saskatchewan and Dakota, Manitoba and Dakota, and Manitoba and Minnesota to the northwest angle of the Lake of the Woods. That is the forty-ninth parallel. From there the line follows a certain described boundary.
What is the length of the line of the forty-ninth parallel which has to be delimited altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Between 750 and 800 miles?
How much has been done?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Four hundred and ten miles in British Columbia, and they have just started this way.

As we have it, there are 390 miles between New Brunswick and the United States, 60 miles between Quebec and New York, 100 miles between Quebec and Vermont, and 750 miles on the forty-ninth parallel. Then we come to the northern trend. What is the delimitation in British Columbia and north?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Alaska coast survey is about 500 miles altogether, of which about one-half has been done. It has been done in sections rather than continually from end to end.
Is that the whole?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of the 141st meridian between Alaska and the Yukon, which is about 500 miles in length, of which 130 miles has been completed. There is water delimitation beyond the 49th parallel. The 49th parallel commences the water delimitation at the Lake of the Woods.
Take all of these first lines which seem to have been sufficient in time past to prevent troubles, what has arisen to make it necessary that there should now be undertaken a new delimitation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The line between New Brunswick and Maine, in fact the line generally from the Ste. Croix river to the St. Lawrence, was surveyed many years ago. Since then many of the survey marks have become obliterated through age; besides, the boundary at the time the survey was made was not very well defined. During more recent years, owing to the lack of definite boundaries, there have been facilities for smuggling and defrauding the revenue on both sides of the line, chiefly by means of building houses on the boundary line itself, and where that line is not well defined, this leads to a good deal of difficulty in suppressing the practice. This accumulation of circumstances necessitated a new survey of the boundary from one end to the other and that has been agreed upon.
Is the United States bearing its share of the cost of this delimitation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Each country has to make Its own survey. We make our survey and their survey checks ours; they make their survey and our survey checks theirs. They would not accept our survey, nor would we accept theirs. So the two parties work together, checking each other as the work' progresses. That is the reason why. as the hou. gentleman said, that the United States party was held up until our party could get in the field. That was the case with regard to the survey of the 141st meridian, and is also the case with regard to this survey between New Brunswick and Maine. The survey has to be made jointly by parties of the two countries, and unless and until our party is in the field, the United States party cannot go on with their work.
Does it in the end cost twice as much for the two countries as it would cost for a single survey?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Approximately it does cost twice as much, but not actually; because, even if Canada were making a survey alone by our party, its work would have to be checked by another party, which would mean a certain amount of expense.
But that is not equal to the first survey?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I say the fact that the two countries do not absolutely trust each other does practically double the cost of the survey, but not altogether.

It seems to me this could be done ; 'Supposing Canada undertook to delimit 100 miles. Its men and methods are known, and it is understood that approximately they are going to make a true and honest survey, is it not possible for the checking to be done by the United States in the case of that 100 miles that the Canadian survey is doing; by the appointment of one or two of their men to accompany our party and act as a check over the work of the Canadian survey? And would it not be possible for Canada to do the same with reference to a hundred miles that the United States survey was carrying out? I should think they* could act as an almost positive check on each other, and thereby the cost would be almost one-half of what it is going to be under the present system. Is that impossible?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is not at all impossible.
Why can't that be done?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman would have to address at least one-half of his inquiry to the government of the United Stated. In the case of the Alaska coast survey, the system the hon. gentleman suggests is followed, as I have already stated; that is, one country makes a survey of a Mr. FOSTER.
certain portion of the boundary and the other country checks that survey. But in that case the boundary is absolutely irregular, being fixed by the summit of the mountain ranges ; in these other cases the boundary is scientifically accurate.

Would not that make it more easy? '
"Mr. OLIVER. I am not able to answer that question. I may say that many years ago the Canadian government did provide for the delimitation of the boundaries of the 141st meridian where it follows the Yukon river between Alaska and the Yukon. Many years afterwards it was found that there was a small error in the survey, and owing to the fact that gold mining was going on in that locality, that error led to what might have been serious complications. It is considered that where the question is one >f accuracy, it is important that there diould be absolute confidence on the part if both countries that the survey shall adequately protect the interest of each coun-ry. and for that purpose each country is willing to pay the cost of its own survey larties.

Of course neither coun-ry wants to spend money uselessly and it wotal'd seem to me as a layman that the most difficult part would be that of the Vlaskan boundary where you have to keep he contour of the mountains in view and place your line in accordance with it. That would be much more difficult than where t is a straight line, say on the 49th parallel >f latitude, where there is nothing of that kind to be taken into account. If the two countries can come to an agreement to save *xpense and, do the checking by superior officers in the more difficult case, why'is it lot possible for them to do it on what ippears to be the easier - sections ? This work has only been commenced and the minister will see that it is going to cost a vast amount of money. There are 2,700 to 3,000 miles altogether to be delimited and at the present rate this will run away up Into the millions. It should not be too late yet to see whether the two countries canto! agree to adopt that system of checking >y superior officers so that the gangs would lo the work separately. In that way half the time would be saved, the work would be completed at a much earlier 'date and nearly one-half the expense m7ould be saved.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was in error in stating that the system of having two parties prevailed along the whole line. That is the system on the 141st meridian where an absolutely new survey is being made in a new country, but my information is that in the New Brunswick-Maine survey a single party made up from the two countries carries on the survey and in the case of the 49th parallel in the prairie section which is

now being surveyed the system suggested by my hon. friend is in force. It is divided into 100 mile sections and one section is done by each country with the checking of each such section by surveyors of the other country. -
The checking is not nearly so expensive as the first survey.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it involves some expense but not so much. The reason for the difference in expense is the difference in the conditions in the different sections. On the 141st meridian it is an absolutely new survey in a new country where the ownership of gold mines is in issue so it has been thought advisable that there should be two parties although it is a very expensive country to keep parties in. iii other sections the system varies according to the conditions and the difficulties of the situation.
Could the minister from the experience they have had and the present cost of this work, give an approximate estimate of the total cost of this work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Just at the moment my information is that it is expected to, if not altogether, at least nearly, complete the work in three years at a cost of about $400,000. That would be in addition to the $125,000 here asked for, making $525,000, including this year.

A dispatch appeared in last night's newspapers stating that the International Waterways Commission is meeting in Buffalo in regard to the international boundary between Canada and the United States through the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence river. This is a very serious matter and I would like to know if the dispatch is at all correct.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The information might be correct. The new treaty provides that the delimitation of the boundary through the St. Lawrence river and the Great Lakes to the mouth of the Pigeon river on the north shore of Lake Superior shall be made by the International Waterways Commission. In that connection the dispatch may be correct.

That part of the boundary which passes through the Niagara river, connecting Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, is of very vital importance. Every foot of it is of very great value to either country and a determined effort has been made by the United States people to make out that the boundary should be in the middle of the river. There may be, I am afraid, a disposition on the part of the Canadian members of the Waterways Commission to concede a sort of compromise. In these deals between the United States and Canada the American people generally manage to ask something extreme and get a compromise which in itself is more than they are entitled to. They are very good
bluffers in that respect and the people in the Niagara district are very much worked up on account of this disposition of the Americans. They apparently feel they have an easy crowd to deal with and they are attempting to get the boundary line there, where it is of great value, over into the river much nearer the Canadian side than it should be. The report of Dr. Spencer, lately published, gives a great deal of information and these people are more or less attacking it. I am afraid that if the government is not very careful a report will be made by the Waterways Commission agreed to by the Canadian section-I do not suggest that they would intentionally sacrifice Canada's rights-without having gone into all the facts as they ought to go into them before making a recommendation to this House. The boundary line between Niagara Falls and Niagara on the Lake and Buffalo, particularly along the part known as the Falls section in which the falls occur, is of the greatest importance, every foot is valuable and the question is one that will produce a great deal of difficulty hereafter if it is not very carefully dealt with. I would really think that at this moment, until they get more complete information, it would not be wise for the International Waterways Commission to undertake to say where the boundary should be.
I do not believe that they have proper data from our side of the case, and I do know that the Americans have been assiduously, for two or three years, working up evidence in the most careful way, surveying our side of the river, and I am afraid they will put professional men in the witness box who will, of course, give evidence on the side they are called upon. These American surveyors would not tell anything in favour of Canada. They have been allowed to survey the river on both sides, a free hand has been given them and they will be able to fortify their theories by what they will call corroborative evidence, and they will go into the witness box and give evidence in a way that I do not think is quite fair to Canada. I am afraid the Waterways Commission has not the evidence or information that it should have to deal with this question. I thought it was wise, as the question of boundaries is before the House, to draw the minister's attention to it, to sound a note of warning as to the matter and to indicate that the Waterways Commission ought not to be allowed to go very fast in deciding that question on the evidence it has at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think that anybody could take any other view than that which my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) has taken, that the question of the boundary, particularly at that point, is one of the very highest importance, and that it is necessary that the interests of Canada should be properly protected. However, this is not a

matter under the administration of the Department of the Interior. The Waterways Commission is apnurtenant to the Department of Public Works.
It was under your department, was it not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
I thought this was the proper place to mention it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The director of the geological survey was a member of the Waterways Commission. However, I am indebted to the hon. gentleman for mentioning this point, and I have no doubt that attention will be paid to it.

This treaty that we have before us specifically provides that the Waterways Commission shall do part of this work. Article 4 reads :
The high contracting parties agree that the existing International Waterways Commission, constituted by concurrent action of the Dominion of Canada and the United States, and composed of three commissioners on the part of the Dominion of Canada and three commissioners on the part of the United States, is hereby authorized and empowered to ascertain and re-establish accurately the location of the international boundary line, beginning at the point of its intersection with the St. Lawrence river near the forty-fifth parallel of north latitude, as determined under Articles I. and VI. of the treaty of August 9, 1812, between Great Britain and the United States, and thence through the great lakes and communicating waterways to the mouth of Pigeon river, at the western shore of Lake Superior, in accordance with the description of such line in Article II. of the treaty of peace between Great Britain and the United States, dated September 3, 1183, and of a portion of such line in Article II. of the treaty of August 9, 1842, aforesaid, and as described in the joint report, dated June 18, 1822, of the commissioners appointed under Article VI. of the treaty of December 24, between Great Britain and the United States, with respect to a portion of said line, and as marked on charts prepared by them and filed with said report, and with respect to the remaining portion of said line as marked on the charts adopted as treaty charts of the boundary under the provisions of Article II. of the treaty of 1842 above mentioned, with such deviation from said line, however, as may be required on account of the cession by Great Britain to the United States of the portion of Horse Shoe Reef, in the Niagara river, necessary for the lighthouse erected there by the United States in accordance with the terms of the protocol of a conference held at the British foreign office, December 9, 1850, between the representatives of the two governments and signed by them, agreeing upon such cession; and it is agreed that wherever the boundary is shown on said charts by a curved line along the water, the commissioners are authorized in their discretion to adopt, in place of such curved line, a series of connecting straight lines defined by distances and courses, and following generally the course cf such curved Mr. OLIVER.
line, but conforming strictly to the description of the boundary in the existing treaty provisions, and the geographical co-ordinates of the turning points of such line shall be stated by said commissioners so as to conform to the system of latitudes and longitudes of the charts mentioned below, and the said commissioners shall, so far as practicable, mark the course of the entire boundary line.
The commission, which is appointed under the present treaty, is laying down the line of demarcation. It is all to go on at the same ' time. There is first the portion . starting at the mouth of the Ste. Croix river down at the Atlantic ocean and crossing I'assamaquoddy bay. Then the work proceeds westward from the mouth to the source of the Ste. Croix river, then to where the 49th parallel crosses the River St. Lawrence, westward through the great lakes to Pigeon river, from Pigeon river to the northwest angle of the Lake of the Woods, thence to the Pacific ocean and finally to the boundary between Alaska and the territory of Yukon. I take it that it is all mixed up together. The commissioners already appointed must jointly do this work and it does seem to me that this House is scarcely as well informed as it ought to be with regard to these provisions where it Interests us above all other things to know what provision is made for delimiting this boundary and what precautions have been taken by the government to see that it is carried out in accordance with the provisions of these treaties, and that we have eminent men appointed to look after Canada's interests. X still think that the House ought to have from some minister of the Crown a comprehensive statement as to what is contemplated to be done and what we commit ourselves to before we commence the work.
Mr. POSTER, Was there any. map presented with this treaty or is there any map which shows the general outline of what the old boundary was and what the new boundary is as it has been laid down ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no map that I am aware of accompanying the copies of the treaty which have been prepared for distribution. The treaty is not a matter appertaining to my own department and therefore I am not in a position to give the information in regard to it that I otherwise would. We are only dealing with the parts of the boundary which have been provided for by previous treaties and which are confirmed by this treaty.
As I understand, this includes all the previous treaties and makes a final definite agreement ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Will this money be used in regard to what I spoke of ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the money we are asking for is simply the delimitation of the land boundary. Our department has nothing to do with the water boundary. This money is required to carry out the work under agreements entered into and treaties made on a previous occasion. We will have to ask for money to enable ns to do our part of the delimitation under the new treaty.
What is the general purpose of this astronomical branch which has 16 high class officials? What have they done so far and what do they propose doing in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The modern science of astronomy represents the accumulated learning of all the ages since the world began, and, therefore, it would be impossible for me-not being acquainted with that science-to give the House any very full account of the operations of the observatory. It is possible to locate definitely any certain point on the earth's surface by knowing the location of certain points in the heavens. The stars are studied partly because of interest in the stars, partly from a purely scientific or speculative point of view, and chiefly in the practical application of their study to defining the location of any point in our country. The work of the branch is divided into several classes. One is purely scientific and speculative; the other is for the purpose of applying the knowledge acquired to the location of fixed points in the geography of our country so that delimitations which have been or may be made upon the ground may be accurately fixed upon the maps. From this feature of the work comes the delimitation of the boundaries of our country which is specially the work of the officers of the astronomical branch who have the scientific knowledge which enables them to absolutely fix any point on the earth's surface. They are the officials upon whom depend the delimitation of our boundaries when a treaty is made which states that a certain line of latitude or longitude is to be followed. We depend upon the practical application of the scientific knowledge of these gentlemen to be sure that the boundary is correctly given. The fixing of geographical points within the country is in the hands of the geodetic survey and the purely scientific work is entirely in the observatory.

Do I understand that we are equipping an observatory and employing a staff of astronomers whose sole idea is to carry on the study of the heavens with the idea of original research so as to advance the science of astronomy purely as a science? What number of officials have we set apart for that work? The thought that comes to one's mind is that this is chiefly the work of great universities and scientific institutions endowed by private benevolence, as is the case in other countries. What is our equipment for this work
which requires such very accurate and costly instruments?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The question my bon. friend asks is difficult to answer in accuracy and detail; but, speaking generally, the answer must be to a certain degree, yes. We are carrying on that original study of the heavens of which he speaks, and which he thinks should be relegated to educational institutions.
I am not so sure that the government should not have something to do with it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is incidental to the necessary practical work of the branch. There are'very few countries in the world which have a longer boundary line or greater area requiring geographical expression than Canada. It is therefore necessary that Canada's equipment for dealing with questions of boundary or geographical location should be large and efficient, in proportion to the wealth and population of the country. Being under the necessity of maintaining an establishment with an equipment on a comparatively large and expensive scale in order to do the practical work, we do in addition and in conjunction with it some part of the educative work-not merely with the idea of adding to the sum of human knowledge of astronomy, but in view of securing greater efficiency in the handling of the practical work. We believe in having what may be called the educative and speculative side of the science in hand in our observatory, because this will enable us to assure the people of Canada better work in the actual delimitation of boundary lines and in the establishment of geogra-pliical points, than would otherwise be the case'. In this, I am informed, w'e are following, I suppose at a very great distance, the example of the British Government in the case of the Royal Observatory at Greenwich.
