There is room for argument that in Canada, where the needs of this special scientific knowledge in its practical application are so great, and where our educational institutions of the higher class are not so amply provided with resources as those of more populous and vastly richer countries, we cannot expect to rely on these educational institutions to the same extent that these other countries do; and therefore, Canada situated as it is, may fairly do rather more in a national way for the purely scientific side of this science, in which the country has such large practical interests, than is done by the United States, whose circumstances are vastly different.

It strikes me that, when it comes to the practical use you are going to make of your astronomical knowledge and your astronomical equipment, it is not necessary to carry on original researches. For instance, the question whether or not

an additional ring can be discovered in some far-off planet, does not liave any relation to your fixing a point geographically on the boundary line. I suppose you fix these points from known data, about which there is no variation. I suppose it is over and above the question of practical utility that you make original researches with your instruments to discover new conjunctions of planets, or new nebulae, or anything of that kind. What you want are the instruments and the men to make fair use of the knowledge you have at your command at present. It is a matter for argument whether we ought to use our staff or our instruments to advance astronomical knowledge in competition with other countries, or how far in that direction we ought to go. I am in favour of Canada taking a leading part in ail such matters. I suppose it is well to have different points of view of the heavens, and you probably do not get all the knowledge you should have by taking all your observations from one country, but get better results by having different points of observation; and that is a fair part of the work for Canada to take part in. But I would think that the practical side of the work would simply require good instruments and good men and accuracy In your calculations. We have extensive boundaries, of course, but we are settling these now, and when they are once settled we are not apt to have them disturbed. In four years time we shall have this whole round finished, and then we shall be pretty clear, so far as international boundaries are [DOT]concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I quite appreciate the view that my hon. friend takes. I have no doubt that it will appeal to a large number of people, and I am bound to say that it appeals to myself in some degree, that we have not any money to throw away on purely scientific enterprises; and I would not like to encourage going beyond a very reasonable limit in regard to purely scientific research in connection with our astronomical branch.
How would your instruments compare in power and intensity with those of large observatories?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They do not compare at all with those of the extraordinary class, but very favourably with those of the ordinary class of observatories. We do not go in for original research in the same degree as those entirely scientific and educational institutions in the United States and some other countries, but we are doing a fair share in the collection of data and the increase of accurate knowledge with regard to the heavenly bodies. No doubt we should be careful not to expend a very large amount, but for the educative value to our own institutions for our own purposes we are warranted in incurring a reasonable Mr. FOSTER.
measure of expenditure in order to keep up the work of original research in the observatory.
How far is the astronomical branch utilized in meteorological research?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has no connection with the meteorological survey. The only purely industrial service it accomplishes is the regulation of the time within the range of its operation.

The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) suggested before recess that it would be well for the government to popularize the knowledge gained by its astronomical staff. Does the minister think that we are getting sufficient new information from this staff to popularize it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the suggestion of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Wm. Roche) is a good one, but we have not taken any steps in that direction yet. The measure of research carried on might very well be given publicity. At present during the *winter months a lecture is given every second week by one of the officers of the observatory to which the public are invited, and these lectures excite a great deal of interest.
That is very local.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but it shows that there is some appreciation of the propriety of the suggestion to publish the work of the observatory. There is quite an active appreciation of that work by the local public.

What is the cost of the observatory ?
Mr.	OLIVER.	The observatory cost
about	$110,000. The buildings are very
substantial and complete. The equipment cost about $50,000.

What is the yearly cost of keeping it up?
Mr.	OLIVER.	Salaries, contingencies,
books and other matters, about $30,000.
Does the librarian give the whole of his duty to that work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He attends to the library and assists in the correspondence.
Mr.	SPROULE. This may be an admirable institution, and ought to be from its cost. We are asked to vote $230,000 in connection with it, a large portion of which will probably be taken to help in delimiting the boundary between Canada and the United States. How is the information obtained to be turned to practical account? The minister's explanations remind me of an old professor's demonstration of chemistry. He said : Take an effervescent, add

a deliquescent, there will be a precipitation, that Is a conglomeration, and that is a demonstration, and is therefore chemistry. The only definite purpose in view seems to be to fix some accurate point on the earth by means of some observations in the heavens. And for that we are spending $130,000 on a building and $30,000 a year to keep it up.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The delimitation of a boundary must start from a point on the earth fixed by observation of the heavens. The work you do on the survey is useless unless there is accuracy in the delimitation.

I admit yon have to fix your post to start from. But J wish to know the return that the country is going to get from this expenditure in a practical way. We wish to know what work is being done for which this large expenditure is asked. Is it a school for educating people in astronomy, or astrology, or experimentation in any scientific direction ? 1 think some person ought to write out an intelligent account of the work that is being done, and how it is likely to benefit Canada, so that it could be read to the House by the minister. We are much like what the minister says of the survey, we want some point to start from.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman does not know where to start from, why does he not stop ?
I am depending on the minister to give us the information, because he is supposed to be the source of knowledge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am sure we appreciate the necessity of having men of scientific knowledge and with the necessary scientific equipment to enable us to meet the experts of the United States in the 'delimitation of these boundaries. I presume that is absolutely essential, and I have no doubt the gentlemen who are connected with that survey are doing good work for the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the ultimate practical purpose of the survey.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is another matter that might be mentioned just now, although it is more by way of suggestion. I observe on page 44 of the report of the Civil Service Commission, this paragraph :
Another important matter which is worthy of consideration is the preparation of maps required by the several departments of the Dominion government. Under the system at present in vogue, maps are prepared by the Departments of Railways and Canals, Marine and Fisheries, Public Works, Militia and Defence, Post Office, Geological Survey and the Department of the Interior. Much praise has been given to an atlas of the Dominion lately prepared by the geographer of the Department of the Interior. Your commissioners would suggest whether it is not possible to group the several officials engaged in this 310
one object under one department and one responsible minister.
It seems to me that is a suggestion which ought to be taken into consideration by the government, more especially by the Department of the Interior, because one would suppose that the gentlemen connected with this particular branch of the Department of the Interior would be those to whom some work of that kind might fittingly be conducted. Then there is another subject I might mention, that is the desirability of having the surveys which are made by the several departments brought under some uniform system, and carried on upon a scientific basis. I believe that every civilized country in the world has a system of what are called geodetic surveys, which are carried out according to very precise and scientific methods, and which are of great value, not only to the government, but to the jjeople who are engaged in various ways in developing the country. I understand this subject has been under the consideration of scientists throughout the country, and I presume it has been under the consideration of the gentlemen who are occupied with this subject in the Department of the Interior ; and I have reason to believe that its desirability has also impressed itself upon the gentlemen who are connected with some of our great educational institutions. I would like to know whether the subject, not only of a uniform system of maps, but of a uniform system of precise and scientific surveys, is engaging the attention of the government, and whether anything is likely to be done along that line in the near future.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The two questions of surveys and map making are not, of course, intimately connected, although they are cognate. The question of combining the map making of all the departments under one department has been under consideration, but so- far no conclusion resulting in the combination of the work has been arrived at. I am not altogether clear that there is all the advantage in such a proposal that the civil service commissioners seem to think. A railway map is compiled for a specific purpose, it has in view a certain object and with that object the employees of the Department of Railways are thoroughly and especially familiar. A map of the same area of country for the Geological Survey would be very different; that department would be interested in different details and it would be only the general scheme map that would be the same. So in any case, as the greater part of the work upon the map is in the details and as the detail work would necessarily have to be done in the department interested in the particular map, there is not a possibility of combining the work of the departments to the extent the commissioners seemed to think. It is possible to combine it to a greater ex-



tent than at present, it is possible that a certain part of the general work on the maps common to all maps covering the same area of country might be done in one branch instead of in several branches, but that would be only a small part of the total work, and would not be the very great advantage that the Civil Service Commissioners seem to think.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There may be, and 4 have no doubt there is, a great deal in what the hon. gentleman observes with regard to the necessary difference of details in maps intended for different purposes. But nevertheless if you had a. uniform scientific survey for the whole country in connection with that proposed map-making department, so that the results of the surveys could be made available for the purpose of all the different departments, you would have a system of maps, whether issued by one department or the other, which would be based upon scientific accuracy. It seems to me that this is of very great importance in Canada. The system to which I aliude has, I understand, been carried out in most European countries and has been carried out to some extent at least in the United States. It would seem to me that the services of this particular department ought to be utilized as far as possible towards bringing about that very desirable result.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The astronomical survey is under way. A section of its work is called the geodetic survey. A part of its employment is as my hon. friend has suggested. We have made a small start in establishing fixed points in different parts of the country by which the surveys already made can be checked up and so more accurate maps can be made than has been possible up to the present time. To make such a geodetic survey for a country of such vast area as Canada within any comparatively short period would cost a stupendous amount of money. In discussing this matter, comparison has been made with England or Belgium or some small European country where there is a large tax-paying power and a small area ; but to attempt to apply to the vast area of the Dominion of Canada the same geodetic survey that has been carried to completion in Belgium, would involve a cost possibly much greater than the advantage to be derived, although everybody must admit that it would be an advantage if we could have it We have started a geodetic survey which is at work in the settled parts of the country and which, as I said, will have the effect of making possible a more accurate system of maps and having more accurate knowledge of the surveys that have been made than we have at present. We are asking parliament of course from year to year for supplies with which to carry on this work, but we are not going into it to Mr. OLIVER.
the extent of undertaking to cover the country within any moderate time The work is so limited in its scope because of the large requirements of money to carry it on that we are subject, I suppose, to criticism from those who think we should have a geodetic survey of the whole country. This is essentially a part of the work of this scientific branch. It is another application of the scientific knowledge which particularly belongs to that branch, which is improved by the scientific research I have mentioned. We expect to have the boundary surveys completed within three of four years, but we will still have need of the same scientific knowledge in carrying forward the work of the geodetic survey, in which all parts of the country are interested and which sometime, no doubt, will be extended over the whole country and the whole country will get the benefit of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suppose the geodetic survey will be able to go on more rapidly after these boundaries have been delimited 1

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We would then feel justified in asking more money for that purpose, but at the present time, when we are asking so much for the boundary survey, we do not feel justified in doing so.
What is the nature of the survey which has been conducted in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The land survey in the west is called a linear survey ; it is merely for the establishment of roads and the setting apart of the country in blocks suitable for settlement. It is approximately astronomically correct but not absolutely. Astronomical correctness is, I might almost say, a secondary consideration, the main thing is to get the country laid out so that people can settle it and use the roads. The geodetic survey will come later and absolutely establish the fixed points in that survey.

I cannot agree with the minister that there is no necessity for an accurate topographical survey of Canada. I think the very example which he has quoted of the two departments having to work over the same ground is in itself an argument in favour of having some organized survey made and the Dominion topographically surveyed. He has merely spoken from the standpoint of the public departments but outside of that of course there are a great many others, the public who want to build railroads or canals who want to get their water supplies or to find out where the- timber areas lie, or what parts of the country are capable of irrigation, have now to undertake independent surveys. All those have at the present time to start out on their own account and undertake individual surveys. They have to examine large tracts of country in preliminary surveys and when they find that their first

attempts are of no use they have to cast them aside and in this way they sustain a great deal of unnecessary loss. They have to undertake experimental surveys until they find a country that is suitable for their undertaking. The whole of that would be obviated if a topographical survey were instituted and carried on methodically. There appear to be six different departments which are carrying on systems of survey. Those systems of survey must overlap in many particulars. A great deal of the work which the department itself is doing must be lost and there must be a considerable duplication of work. I understand that some of the important bodies which occasionally meet, such as the Royal Society and the Canadian Society of Civil Engineers, have strongly recommended to the government that there should be a topographical survey. It would mean an immense saving to the people as well as to the government. I would like to ask the minister if he could give any idea of the amount of money which is spent on surveys by the different departments of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the faintest idea.
I presume that the surveys approximate very nearly $1,000,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The surveys of the Interior Department alone amount to more than $1,000,000.
The surveys of the Interior Department alone ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. We asked for $800,000 last year for land surveys and something over $200,000 for astronomical surveys.

What is the approximate cost per mile of making a topographical survey of country such as we find in Canada?
' Mr. OLIVER. A geodetic survey has been in operation for two years and this has cost the country over $50,000. We have run a belted triangulation from Quebec to London, Ont. This triangulation would be the basis of a topographical survey. It will take another year to cover the ground between Quebec and London in order to perfect the triangulation and then the work of the topographical survey will go on. The triangulation fixes the points and the geographical survey fills in the details.
(Mr. LAKE. I imagine that a topogra-graphical survey cannot be exceedingly expensive. We have had maps supplied to us which were drawn up by the Department of Militia and Defence, very excellent maps, which gave all the natural features of the country and I imagine that such a topographical survey as that would be all that would be needed for this country. I 310J
cannot imagine that that could be so very expensive because I do not think that the estimates for that survey in the Department of Militia and Defence are very great. It seems to me. that a great deal of the money which we spend on the duplication of surveys is being wasted. How much have these surveys in the Northwest, for which we are paying $800,000 a year, cost per square mile?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that question at the moment. If my hon. friend wants to know what is the total number of acres surveyed in the Northwest by this linear survey I will tell him that it Is 120,000,000 acres.

All that country will have to be gone over again some day with a topographical survey. Of course, I agree that it is necessary to get the work done at once by this rough and ready survey which probably will have to be very frequently corrected and which may lead to a good deal litigation. I think that under the present system we are liable to have a great deal of litigation in many parts of Canada from not having a very accurate survey. I cannot help thinking that the minister is making a mistake in not using his influence with the rest of the members of the government to have one general survey department established which would carry on a complete topographical and geodetic survey of the Dominion. It would be a great saving to the government and to the public generally.
Mr. OLIVER, The question my hon. friend raises has been under consideration. The difficulty in the way is the immense area of country the immediate requirements of which in regard to surveys have to be immediately provided for. It is desirable to build a railway in a certain locality and we cannot wait for a geodetic survey in order to build that railway. We have to make a linear survey to provide for the settlement of the country. Although we asked parliament last year for $800,000 and we are asking this year for an equal, or possibly a larger amount, we still owing to the enormous territory and the rapidity of settlement, are unable to provide, in all cases, for the requirements of the people who desire to push out into the farther and farther country. I would be afraid to ask parliament for the money that would be necessary to cover that country within a reasonable time with a triangulated survey such as we have been carrying on in eastern Canada. We could not keep settlers waiting until such a survey could be made to accommodate them. Our area is so great and our needs are such that we must meet these needs as thev arise without waiting for a survey which in itself is entirely desirable, but which our circumstances do not admit of our having.

I frankly admit there is necessity for going ahead with the linear survey in the Northwest and that if you want to build a railway into a remote district you cannot wait to have a topographical survey made. But if a topographical survey had been going on for some years past the probability is that the location of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the maritime provinces, for instance, would have been already surveyed and the general route of the railway derived from it so that the necessity would have been obviated of striking out several different experimental lines before you could locate the exact line on which you are to run your railway. In that way the duplication of work would be avoided.

Article 1 of this treaty provides that an expert geographer or surveyor shall be appointed by each country without delay to more correctly define the international boundary between the Dominion and the United States in the waters of Passamaquoddy bay, and Articles 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 provide for a similar commission. Is it intended to appoint separate commissions for the different sections or will the same commissioners do all the work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is outside the work of my department, but should think that under the treaty the appointments should be made forthwith. The second last paragraph of article 9 provides :
It is understood that under the foregoing articles the same persons will he appointed to carry out the delimitation of the boundaries in the several sections aforesaid.
Therefore it would appear that one man from each country shall constitute the commission for the whole boundary line, with the exception mentioned in section 4.
Can the minister give any idea of how long it will take two men to fix that boundary which is, I suppose, 4,000 miles long?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I presume that commission would direct the workings of different parties in the different places.
Would they have subordinate surveyors to do the actual surveying ?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely.
I thought we were told that one of the most eminent surveyors in the country was actually engaged with his assistants in the work of surveying through the mountains.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Was that said to-day ?
No, some years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I understand it the intention is that the whole of the boundary line, except that part which has been assigned to the Waterways Commission, shall Mr. OLIVER.
be adjusted by the two commissioners who shall direct the work.

Do they remain at headquarters ?
Mr. OLIVER, If in case their personal presence was required at any point I suppose they would go there, but otherwise I presume they would be at headquarters.

That was not the information that was given us some years ago. The member for Vancouver told us the Americans had their surveying parties out there already, but I saw it stated some time ago that the American parties remained there all winter as it was too expensive to bring them out and that the Canadian parties would join them in the spring.	-	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is perfectly correct in regard to the work of making the surveys ; but under this treaty the commissioners are to see that the work is done and the boundary properly located.
What surveyors are being sent out to do this work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are not sending any surveyors out on the surveys that will be necessary under the terms of this treaty. We have not yet asked parliament fpr the money to enable us to send them out, and we are not of course prepared to send them dntil parliament vote's us the necessary money.

What do you mean by the demarcation of the boundaries ? Is not that surveying ?
Mr. OLIVER, The surveys for which we are now asking parliament for money are not the surveys to be decided upon by the commission. The surveys now going on are not because of this treaty, but because of a treaty made in former years.
Who are making those surveys ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The names of the surveyors whom we propose to employ under the vote we are now asking the House for are: On the 141st meridian boundary, A. J. Bra-bazon, D. H. Nelles, F. Lambart; on the Alaska coast boundary, J. D. Craig, W. F. Ratz, George White-Fraser, F. H. Mackie ; on the 49th parallel, J. J. McArthur, N. J. Ogilvy ; on the New Brunswick and Maine boundary, G. C. Rainboth.
Who is the supervising commissioner ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The commissioner to be appointed under the treaty has not been appointed yet.
Under whose supervision is the work being done that has been going on for some time ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. King is directing that survey on behalf of Canada. If a dispute arises, that dispute is to be settled under the terms of the treaty by two commissioners to be appointed.
They have been working for years, and surely there have been differences of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what the treaty is for-to adjust those differences of opinion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister for an explanation of the decrease of $14,000 in this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is due to slackening up the work a little on the 49th parallel.
Salaries of agents and employees, in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries, $200,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, in the absence of the Minister of Militia, whether or not it. is intended to hold militia camps in the month of June ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the absence of the Minister of Militia I regret I cannot give an answer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is the minister available ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is in the city and was present to-day. I do not know where he is at the moment.
Who is the government immigration agent in St. Paul ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Holmes.

Is the government aware that charges have been made in the public press to the effect that certain Dominion lands agents and immigration agents were acting as selling agents of lands for certain lands companies. I have heard that some of the agents in the United States were acting for the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company and directing homesteaders to the lands particularly owned by that or some other companies, in whose behalf they were acting. Has the hon. minister any information on that subject ? I brought this matter to his attention some time ago.
Mr. OLIVER'. I think I remember my hon. friend bringing that matter to my attention and I made inquiries, but so far have not been able to substantiate the charges made.

Since I brought the question up last, I have received a clipping from the Minneapolis ' Journal ' of April 26 containing this advertisement :
Fifty thousand acres of Southern Alberta land for sale in blocks of 5,000 acres up. Canadian office, St. Paul.
That would look as if the immigration agent in St. Paul were acting as selling agent for this Southern Alberta Land Company. At any rate the party who sent me this is fully convinced that he is, and he thinks it would be entirely unwise for immigration agents of the Canadian government to be acting for land companies and throwing the weight of their official position in behalf of any particular land company, a position I heartily concur in.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would my hon. friend kindly send me over that clipping ?
Has the government as many agents in Great Britain and Europe this year as last and is it the intention to continue having as many ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the same number as last year.
How many are there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Twenty-seven employees of all classes in Great Britain and Ireland and four on the continent. ,
Are there not in addition agents specially sent on temporary engagements for three or six months and how many are there ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, something over twenty such agents went last year and we expect to send a similar number this coming fall.
Are they subject to the agents already there ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are subject to the orders of the resident agent. Their business is to give personal experience of the desirability of Canada as a field for settlement. So far we have selected successful farmers who came originally from some part of the old country, as we think that the appearance of such and their statements are the best argument we can offer in favour of Canada as a field for settlement.
On what basis are they paid?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are expected to account for their actual expenses in addition to the salary we pay them. We pay them $100 a month for the time they are absent and their actual travelling expenses.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. McLEAN (Prince Edward Island).
speechtext:
I note that Mr. McLaughlin, who was sent to secure immigrants to the maritime provinces, has only sent one so far to that section, although he has been on the other side two years. The probability is that he is working to promote emigration to western Canada. Have the government changed their idea of having him represent the maritime provinces? What instructions were given Mr. McLaughlin regarding the territory he has to represent when sending immigrants to Canada? The maritime

provinces should receive some consideration. I do not think that immigrants should be exclusively sent to western Canada. The government should take some steps to promote settlement in the maritime provinces and Quebec. The agent in the old country is likely to exaggerate the advantages of the western country and to neglect eastern Canada. If the government send these maps to the different schools and other places in the old country to be exhibited, they ought to give due importance to the maritime provinces on those maps, and instruct their agents to send immigrants to eastern Canada as well as to western Canada. I think there should be a more equal distribution of the immigration to this country, and that the immigrants should be told that they will receive just as good treatment and will fiDd just as great advantages in eastern Canada as in western Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In regard to Mr. McLaughlin, he was employed two years ago especially to represent Prince Edward Island in the old country. It was believed that there was in the island a field for immigrants by reason of the rush of the native inhabitants to the west, and that there might be people in the old country who would wish either to become purchasers of farms in the island or tenants. Mr. McLaughlin did work in the old country for about two years, and I regret to say that his efforts have not been successful. At the present time I think he is no longer connected with the Immigration Department. We are considering the subject of dealing further with the question of immigration to Prince Edward Island, as well as to the other maritime provinces. I would like to say that so far as my knowledge goes, the maps we send to the old country or anywhere else give an equal share of prominence and publicity to the island, and give its area according to the best knowledge we have of geography. Recently we have published a further edition of our map of Canada for the use of schools in which we give special prominence to the maritime provinces.

I do not think it would be fair to Mr. McLaughlin to allow the statements of the Minister of the Interior to pass without remark. I do not think it would be fair to any representative of the maritime provinces to say that he did not do his duty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not say Mr. McLaughlin did not do his duty ; I said he was not successful.
Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Supply, in the same department.
House adjourned at six o'clock.
Thursday, June 4, 1908.
